item.title: Version 3.0.4
item.description:
RetroMac 3.0.4

New

  • SETI@home Classic, simulated. The 1999–2005 client as a window and as a screensaver (Settings ▸ Themes ▸ Screensaver ▸ SETI@home, and the saver picker): a work unit is "received", analysed pass after pass — baseline smoothing, FFTs at changing resolution and drift, the search for Gaussians, pulses and triplets — and "sent back", and the counters climb as the client's did. Windows 95 to XP get the Windows client 3.08 (in the Start menu), System 7.1 and Mac OS 9 the Macintosh client 2.01 with its green telescope in the menu bar, Mac OS X 10.0 a reconstruction of the Mac OS X client with its first start (Preferences, then Login). The window, the background and the saver share one work unit, saved between launches; it runs only while shown, or also in the background if you choose, and never while the Mac sleeps. Now and then a strong peak turns up and is examined, as a Gaussian, pulse or triplet when that is what the client was searching for; it never claims anything was found, and can be switched off or set rarer or more often. Historical and demonstration speed (a unit in about four minutes). The main view is measured off two contemporary screenshots; the logo, menus and dialogs are reconstructions, listed in docs/SETI.md. The graphs stay up through every step of the analysis, and the screensaver fills the screen. Nothing is analysed and nothing goes over the network.
  • SETI@home on the Windows desktops. Windows 95, 98, Me and XP have a SETI@home icon on the desktop and in the Start menu's Programs, and the window wears it in its title bar.
  • A screensaver ends on purpose. A small nudge of the mouse no longer ends it, and the click that does stays on the screensaver instead of landing on the window underneath.
  • Stacks show everything. A dock folder's stack no longer stops at 40 entries: the grid scrolls, and a folder in it opens inside the stack, with a back arrow at the top left. The arrow keys move through it, Return opens, Esc closes.
  • Fan, Grid and List. A folder's right-click has 10.6's Sort by (Name, Date Added, Date Modified, Date Created, Kind), Display as (Folder or Stack) and View content as (Fan, Grid, List, Automatic). Automatic fans out while everything fits above the dock and shows the grid beyond that, as Snow Leopard did. The fan is there on Snow Leopard and Mountain Lion with the dock at the bottom.
  • Exposé, as in 10.6. Space shows the highlighted window at full size, the arrow keys move between windows and Return brings one forward. Held on a dock icon, Exposé lists the app's minimised windows in a row of their own along the bottom (needs Accessibility). On close the windows fly back to where they are.
  • Launchpad keeps your order. Drag an icon to move it, the others make room; hold it at the left or right edge to take it to the next page. The order stays, and apps installed later join at the end. Apps in a folder of Applications, such as Utilities, are in the grid now too, and the arrow keys move through it, Return opens.
  • About This Mac of Mac OS X 10.0 and About This Computer of Mac OS 9. Their Apple menus open the windows of their day, filled with this Mac: the blue X over "Mac OS X" with version, build, memory and processor; the Mac OS face over "Mac OS 9" with version, memory, virtual memory, the largest unused block, and the open apps with a bar for the memory each holds. Laid out off 10.0.4 and 9.0; the logos are redrawn, not copied.
  • Location in the Apple menu lists the Mac's own network locations with the one in use ticked, and picking another switches to it (Mac OS X 10.0 and Snow Leopard).

Fixes

  • Downloads and Applications left the Windows taskbars. Pinned by a theme with stacks (Snow Leopard, Mountain Lion), they are taken out again in a theme without them. RetroMac and RetroMac Dev share one dock list but remembered separately which folders they had pinned, so the other one's Downloads and Applications stayed in the quick launch and the Start menu. The mark now sits on the item itself, and either app's note counts.
  • Snow Leopard's desktop says Exposé, with its accent.
  • Location no longer claims "Automatic" on every Mac; the tick sat there whatever was set.
  • Files dropped into a framed window went nowhere. The frame RetroMac draws round every window (Windows, NeXTSTEP, CDE, Photon, Mac OS X themes) was a window as large as the one it framed, transparent inside, and drag-and-drop took it as the target: moving or copying by drag into a Finder window did nothing, with no error. The frame's window is now only the ring (reported by a user on Windows 95/98 and NeXTSTEP).
  • The floating button keeps clear of the theme's dock. Placed bottom right by default, it sat on NeXTSTEP's recycler and over the Windows taskbar; it now steps aside of the dock or taskbar until you drag it somewhere yourself.
  • Automation showed as off although it was on. Settings asked macOS while System Events was not running, and macOS then answers "no such app" whatever the permission. RetroMac starts System Events quietly first (reported on a Mac mini M4).
  • RetroMac could crash when switching themes. The dock closed its watch on the Trash twice; the second close could hit a file another part of RetroMac had just opened, and reading it then ended the app ("Bad file descriptor", reported from the menu bar's theme switch).
  • Time Machine restores work again with Classic Finder on. Its themes also set the Mac's sidebar corner radius (NSSplitViewItemGlassMinimumCornerRadius) for every app, and with it a restore showed as done but put nothing back. RetroMac no longer sets it and puts back the user's own value on the next theme switch or launch (reported on macOS 27.2 with Windows 98).
  • Window frames and title bars no longer flash in Photos. RetroMac took any element an app removes for a closed window; Photos removes its player's views when a video is selected, and the frame and bar of its window went and came back. A window now counts as gone only when the WindowServer no longer has it (reported with Windows 9x and Mac OS 8 Copland).
  • A click on the desktop brings the Finder to the front, as on the Mac. RetroMac's desktop icon layer took the click.
  • The log keeps a crash's last lines at its end. Error output started writing at the top of the log file and overwrote its first lines.
  • One launcher at a time. With RetroMac in the Dock, its Dock icon and the floating button each opened their own launcher, and both could be on screen at once. Opening one now closes the other.

item.title: Version 3.0.3
item.description:
RetroMac 3.0.3

New

  • Snow Leopard's Apple menu. The Apple in the menu bar opens the menu of Mac OS X 10.6, row for row, instead of today's system menu: About This Mac, Software Update, Mac OS X Software, System Preferences, Dock, Location, Recent Items, Force Quit with the name of the front app, Sleep, Restart, Shut Down and Log Out with your full name. Force Quit opens the Force Quit window and ends nothing on its own.

Fixes

  • Switching apps from the dock. A click on a running app's tile did nothing while another app was in front: since macOS 14 an app in the background may no longer bring another to the front. The window server does it now, and it needs no permission.
  • VoiceOver and the menu-bar menu. Since 3.0 VoiceOver saw RetroMac's icon as a plain button, the menu never opened and the focus fell to the Apple menu or the desktop. While VoiceOver runs the menu hangs on the icon again, as it did before 3.0.
  • Dock magnification cut the icons off. Turned on while the dock was up, the icons grew but the dock's window kept its old height, and they ended at its top edge.
  • Mountain Lion's folders in the dock. Applications is a folder again rather than a pile of the apps last installed, and a folder in the Downloads pile is a folder of its time, not today's flat blue one.

item.title: Version 3.0.2
item.description:
RetroMac 3.0.2

New

  • Sounds. A new place in Settings for a Mac that makes no sound of its own: keys that click (subtle, clicky or a typewriter, with the bell on Return), a hard drive that spins up, seeks when the disk is really busy and parks when you turn it off (six drives from a 1986 stepper to a 15K server, synthesized by Platter's DriveSynth), and a fan that rises with the CPU load and runs on after it. One master switch and volume, everything off until you turn it on. It pauses while a microphone records, the screen is shared, the Mac is muted or asleep, and follows the output device. The drive counts disk activity and nothing else; the keyboard learns only which kind of key went down, never what was typed, and needs Accessibility.
  • Start menu search in Windows 7 and Vista. Type while the Start menu is open and the search box takes it, as on the real thing: the left pane shows the installed programs that match, a sum worked out (12*3, Return copies the answer) and a web address to open (github.com). Return opens the first match, the box's × clears it. The keys are held only while the menu is open and read through your keyboard layout. After Startish.
  • Start with a tap of Left ⌘. As the Windows key did: press and let go of the left Command key on its own and the Start menu opens; Command shortcuts work as before. Off by default, under Settings ▸ Themes ▸ Dock on themes with a Start button.
  • Right-click on a taskbar button. Windows 95 to XP show the window's system menu (Restore, Minimize, Maximize, Close); Windows 7 the foot of its jump list: the program, pin or unpin it, close the window.
  • NeXTSTEP title bars and miniwindows. With the theme's title bars on, every window under the NeXTSTEP theme wears the NeXT bar: black on the key window, grey on the others, the miniaturize button at the left end and close at the right. A miniaturized window leaves a miniwindow on the workspace, as NeXTSTEP did: a tile with the app's icon under a black strip with the window's title, along the bottom of the screen from the Dock leftwards; double-click it to put the window back.
  • Square corners everywhere at once. A theme with its own title bars makes windows square, but an app only takes that on when it starts. Picking such a theme now offers to restart the open apps: they are listed to leave some out, each is asked to quit the normal way (so it can ask about unsaved work), and opened again. With "Don't ask again". Not asked at launch, nor when the corners stay as they were.
  • Aero Snap, Shake and Peek in Windows 7. Drag a window by its title bar to the left or right edge and it fills that half of the screen, to the top and it fills the screen, with Windows 7's glass preview while you hold it there; drag it away and it has its old size back. Ctrl+Option+arrows do the same from the keyboard. Shake a window and every other app hides; shake it again and they return. The taskbar has its Show Desktop strip at the right end again: rest the pointer on it and the windows turn to glass outlines over the desktop, click it and the desktop shows. Each has its switch under Settings ▸ Themes ▸ Windows 7 extras; Snap and Shake need Accessibility.
  • Windows stay clear of the dock. As on the real systems, a window that comes to rest under the retro dock or taskbar moves out from under it, or gets shorter when it does not fit. It looks once a window has settled, never during a drag, and gives up on a window that keeps going back, so it never fights you or an app. On by default; Settings ▸ Themes ▸ Dock.
  • The Command Prompt in Terminal. Under the Windows themes Terminal's prompt reads C:\Users\you> instead of you@Mac ~ %. zsh still runs your own startup files, unchanged; RetroMac only sets the prompt after them and edits nothing in your home folder. Only when your login shell is zsh; after macOS 7 Ultimate SP1's cmd-zsh.
  • Device chime. Under Windows XP, Vista and 7 a chime sounds when a USB device is plugged in or pulled out (one per device, none for the devices that drop and return when the Mac wakes). Only while RetroMac's sounds are on and macOS's "Play user interface sound effects" is too; Settings ▸ Sounds ▸ Interface sounds.
  • Desktop Games in RetroHub ▸ Apps. The Gemtree stress reducer of 2000, ported to the Mac by ucodia: it takes a picture of your screen and lets you wreck it with a hammer, chain-saw, machine gun, flame-thrower, termites and more, then wash it clean. Once installed it sits on the Windows 95, 98, Me and XP desktops as stress.exe, the name it had.

Fixes

  • Switching apps from the taskbar. A click on another app's button brought its window up only inside that app, behind the one in front: since macOS 14 an app in the background may no longer bring another to the front. The window server does it now, for the window switcher too.
  • Mac OS 8 and 9: inactive title bars are flat, without pinstripes and boxes, as the real ones were, and a click there only brings the window forward; RetroMac's own windows too.

item.title: Version 3.0.1
item.description:
RetroMac 3.0.1

New

  • New theme: Mac OS 8 (Copland). The Mac OS that never shipped, as Apple's June 1996 developer release D11E4 showed it: the purple grid desktop, lavender folders, Platinum windows and menus in their first form, drives top right and the Trash bottom right, no dock and no Control Strip. Its pattern, icons and nine more desktop patterns are D11E4's own, decoded from the resource forks of its files. Its title bars wear D11E4's own close, zoom and collapse boxes (the system's 'pixs' pictures, with their pressed state), and an inactive window loses its stripes and boxes as it did there; a click on one only brings it forward. It starts with D11E4's own start-up, the Mac OS face built square by square, has an Applications folder on the desktop in its look, and a window minimised with ⌘M zooms away the Mac OS 8 way instead of shrinking towards a hidden Dock. RetroMac's own windows (Applications, Calculator, Notepad, Clock, CPU) wear D11E4's boxes, scroll arrows and the lavender thumb, one arrow at each end, flat when inactive.
  • RetroHub. The Game & Apps Library is now RetroHub, with a third tab: Themes, for themes that are not built in. The list comes from the RetroMac repository, so a new theme needs no app update; each download is checked against the list's SHA-256 and installed like a theme opened from the Finder. RetroHub and Themes have their own pixel icons in the menu.
  • Badges on dock icons, where the system had them. Mail's unread count and every other app's number show on the retro dock in the themes whose system drew them, the way it drew them: Mac OS X 10.0 only on Mail (Mail painted its own red circle; other apps could not until 10.5), Snow Leopard and Mountain Lion on every app as the glossy red pill, Windows 7 as an overlay on the taskbar button's icon. No other theme shows any. The numbers come from the Mac's own Dock through Accessibility; Settings ▸ Themes ▸ Badges on icons turns them off. From a user's request.
  • Six more in RetroHub ▸ Apps. ICQuel (a late-90s instant messenger), Retrolux (photo library and editing in the style of the Snow Leopard years' pro photo software), Retron Commander (a Norton Commander for the Mac), Macsplorer (the Windows 2000 Explorer as a file browser), ARose (the Amiga's BlitzBlank screen saver, revived with its authors' blessing) and Johnny Castaway (Sierra's 1992 screen saver, on Open Scrantic's reimplementation of its engine). Johnny Castaway needs your own copy of the three original files, asked for and checked the first time; once installed he is in Program Manager's Games group on Windows 3.x and on the desktop of Windows 95, 98 and Me.
  • Dragging a window the way its era did. Mac OS 6 to 9, Windows 3.x, Windows 95 and CDE drag an outline and move the window once, on release; the others move the bar and the patch over the real traffic lights with the window, without the lag that let the lights show.
  • Two new monitors, two truer ones. Orange Plasma is the gas-plasma screen of the laptops around 1990 (IBM P70, #ff6a1a on near-black), White Phosphor the DEC VT100's cool P4 white. Amber Monitor now has the Hercules monitor's P3 amber, and Game Boy SameBoy's measured DMG shades and the slow STN panel, so with Phosphor Glow on a moving picture smears both ways like the real one. All of them turn the picture into its own brightness, so text stays sharp enough to work in. Colours from BURNIN's sources.
  • Windows XP in high resolution. 30 of the XP theme's icons, from My Computer and the Recycle Bin to the Start menu's Run, Search and Turn Off, are now the hand-redrawn versions of marchmountain's Windows XP High Resolution Icon Pack (CC0): sharp on a Retina screen instead of soft at 32 to 64 pixels.
  • RetroHub's apps in the Setup Assistant. A new Apps page lists every app RetroHub offers, with its picture and an Install button, after the Games page. The lone Reframe row on the System page went into it. In the menu, RetroHub now sits on the first level and opens on Apps; Display moved into More.

Fixes

  • RetroHub and Themes show their icons in the menu-bar menu. Their pixel icons were drawn by a handler and came out blank in the menu; they are bitmaps now.
  • Theme menus under the shader. The Apple menu and menu bar menus of the Mac OS themes, CDE's menus and the Control Strip's volume slider opened above the shader, unfiltered, in the middle of a filtered screen. They now lie just under it, like the Start menu.
  • Phosphor Glow fades like the real tube. On the monochrome presets the afterglow now follows the monitor's own phosphor, with RCA's measured times: Amber Monitor's P3 is down to a tenth in 13 ms, Terminal Green's P1 in 24.5 ms, and Green Phosphor's P39, the IBM MDA's, in 150 ms before its long 1/t tail, the famous MDA smear. 100 % is the real tube. On colour presets it stays an effect: a colour tube's phosphor is dark within a millisecond. The glow also no longer leaves a faint residue that never fades. Data via BURNIN (GPL-3).
  • The MS-DOS Prompt is grey again. The Windows themes' Terminal profile was green on black; the real prompt was light grey on black.
  • The taskbar without Accessibility. A program whose last window was closed no longer keeps its button, and clicking a program's button opens it again the way the Dock does, so its window comes back. From a tester.
  • The disk image opens as a proper install window. RetroMac on the left, Applications on the right, an arrow between, on Platinum grey: drag it across. Before, the window took whatever view the Finder was set to.
  • Badges survive a theme switch. Turning a theme on or switching between Snow Leopard and Mountain Lion restarted the Mac's Dock, which forgets every badge, and Mail sends its count again only when it changes. Global tweaks like scroll bars no longer restart the Dock, and after a restart the badges RetroMac had seen stay until the Dock has them again.
  • Desktop Glass is gone again. It was an experiment and should not have shipped in 3.0.
  • Windows 3.x: the icons of running programs can be dragged anywhere on the desktop, as in Windows 3.1, and stay where they were put (per app). A click without moving still brings the program forward; the icons lie under the Program Manager, as Win 3.1's lay under its windows.
  • Themes can be deleted. Settings ▸ Themes ▸ Delete… moves your own or an imported theme to the Trash, after asking; the built-in themes stay. If it was the selected theme, Maik's Favourite takes its place.
  • A .retromactheme opens in RetroMac. A double-click in the Finder installs the theme, selects it and shows it in Settings ▸ Themes; macOS used to say RetroMac cannot open files in that format. "Add custom…" accepts a theme or a .zip with one (the panel only took folders, so a theme could not be chosen), and a failed import says why. A folder that only has the extension is refused instead of being installed as a broken theme.

item.title: Version 3.0
item.description:
RetroMac 3.0

New

  • New theme: Halloween. A dark, grimy glass dock — smears, drips, dust — with a smouldering fire round it: a charred edge with embers glowing up and dying down, a flickering red heat, small flames, sparks and smoke rising from the top (still under Reduce Motion). The dock arches up over a magnified icon like a band laid over it and stays clear of the Live Wallpaper; the jack-o'-lantern in place of the Apple, dark mode with an orange accent, and a Halloween night for the wallpaper (three to choose from, changed with a right-click on the desktop), a kitchen knife for the pointer, and with the title bars on, three glowing fireballs in place of the traffic lights, where Macintosh HD and your Desktop folder stand. The pumpkin is also a menu-bar Apple style of its own. With Match appearance on, macOS tints every app icon in the accent colour (the Tinted icon style of macOS 26 and later), and your own icon style comes back when the theme goes off.
  • See what a theme changes before you turn it on. The theme's page in Settings ▸ Themes lists every change it makes to macOS with your switches as they are — Dock, menu bar, wallpaper, appearance and accent, pointer, Terminal profile, window corners and each Classic Finder setting — as yours → the theme's.
  • Restore my settings. RetroMac now remembers each macOS setting as it was before it first changed it, and Settings ▸ General puts exactly those back: your Finder view, your Dock, your menu bar — not the factory defaults, which "Restore macOS defaults" still offers.
  • A theme on chosen Spaces only. Themes ▸ On This Space in the menu, or Settings ▸ General ▸ Spaces: the theme stays on those Spaces and slides away with them, and the others are plain macOS, with the Mac's Dock, menu bar, cursor and own wallpaper, and the shader paused.
  • New theme: QNX 6.2.1 — Photon. The realtime OS's desktop from its 2003 CD, measured off the original: the shelf down the right with groups you fold open and shut, a live system monitor, the CD player and World View; the taskbar with Launch, one entry per window and the clock; Photon's blue title bars. Every launcher opens a real Mac app or setting, the Launch menu sorts your apps into Photon's categories (add any app to any of them), a right-click on the desktop brings up the same menu, World View opens Mission Control, and the clock, calculator, Notepad and CPU monitor wear Photon's blue title bar.
  • New theme: Solaris 8 — CDE. The Common Desktop Environment as Solaris 8 shipped it in 2000, measured off the original: the Front Panel at the bottom with a live clock, today's date on the calendar and a cpu/disk meter; an arrow over every control opens its subpanel, and an app dropped on "Install Icon" stays there. The mauve dtwm title bars, the tiled Solaris sun on the purple desktop. Every control opens a real Mac app or setting; the four workspaces open Mission Control, and Exit turns the theme off. A right-click on the desktop brings up the Workspace Menu, the box at the left of a title bar its window menu (a double-click closes the window), and a minimised window lies on the desktop as an icon until you restore it. The Application Manager shows your apps in Solaris-style groups (Desktop_Apps, Desktop_Tools …) and all of them in one more, in a window built like CDE's File Manager. The clock, calculator, Notepad and CPU monitor wear dtwm's mauve frame. Crashes come the Solaris way: a BAD TRAP panic on the black-on-white Sun console, a watchdog reset that leaves OpenBoot at its ok prompt, and after a restart fsck asking for the root password.
  • Historic icons for modern apps. A theme can take an icon package: a folder of PNGs with an icons.json saying which app each is for, whether it is the era's own icon or a modern app drawn in its style, and at which sizes. RetroMac checks every file on import, keeps an app's working icon when its new one is broken, and shows the package in the dock and on the theme's panels at once. Settings ▸ Dock ▸ Historic icons shows what is in, in use, missing and broken.
  • Window switcher. ⌃⌥Tab (Shift the other way) does what the theme's era did: Solaris moves the focus to the next window at each press, Snow Leopard opens Exposé, Mountain Lion Mission Control. Eras that had no switcher get none. Change the keys, or leave it off for a theme, in Settings ▸ Shortcuts.
  • Rescue Desktop. One action takes the theme, the shader and every desktop effect away and brings back windows you cannot reach: rolled-up ones, ones parked off screen, ones left on a display that is no longer there. Your settings stay, and a report says what was done, skipped or did not work. ⌃⌥⌘R (change it in Settings ▸ Shortcuts), the flyout, or "Rescue Desktop" in the menu-bar menu. If RetroMac quits mid-rescue, the next start turns nothing on and finishes it; --rescue-desktop on the command line does the same on request.
  • New theme: Windows Vista. Aero glass windows on a black glass taskbar with the round Start orb, Start Search and the orange power button, the time on one line, the Welcome screen at start, eight Vista wallpapers from Aurora to the Ultimate orb, and Vista's own icons from Luximoz's Windows Vista icon pack.
  • The Vista Sidebar. A column on the right edge with a clock, a calendar and a CPU meter whose two dials show your Mac's processor and memory load. The + at its top shows or hides each gadget. "Close Sidebar" (right-click, or the +) puts it away; "Windows Sidebar" in the Start menu brings it back.
  • Windows XP Task Manager, all five pages. Applications lists the running programs (End Task, Switch To, New Task); Processes shows each process with its user, CPU and memory, sorts by any column and ends a process after XP's warning; Networking draws a graph per adapter with its link speed; Users lists who is logged in. "Task Manager" is in the XP Start menu now too.
  • Game & Apps Library. The Game Library has a second tab, Apps: retro-looking Mac apps that are real apps — Reframe, RetroFind, RetroContacts, RetroReminder, RetroCal, RetroNotes, Classic Mac Finder and QuickTune install with one press, from their makers, checked for signature, notarisation and bundle ID; Mojave Paint opens in the Mac App Store. Each card shows the app's own screenshot. Installed, an app is taken off the theme title bars once (it draws its own), also when it came from somewhere else and is first started.
  • Desktop Glass. A window you place over anything — a video, an emulator, a web page — that shows what lies under it through the current shader (ShaderGlass's idea on Windows). It runs with the shader on or off, follows the preset in the menu, remembers where it was, and with Click Through on, the pointer reaches what is under it. Menu-bar menu or Settings ▸ Shader ▸ Screen & Apps.
  • Betas on request. About ▸ Software Updates ▸ "Include beta versions" brings test builds through the regular updater; off, a Mac stays on the released versions.

Known limits

  • The Windows switchers are not in yet. Alt+Tab for Windows 95 to XP and Flip and Flip 3D for Vista and 7 come once their reference screenshots are in; until then ⌃⌥Tab does nothing in those themes. QNX gets no Alt+Tab until it is shown for 6.2.1.
  • No historic icon packages ship with 3.0. The import, the checks and the status view are there; the pictures come as packages of their own.
  • Not yet in the new themes: Solaris's dtlogin screen and X11 cursors, and QNX's boot screen, crashes and cursors. None of them is in the reference screenshots.
  • Window features need Accessibility. The title bars, the window menu, minimised-window icons, the taskbar entries and the switcher work with it; without it the taskbars show apps instead of windows, as before. The title bars are still experimental.
  • On a Space without the theme, the appearance, accent colour, Finder and Terminal changes, square window corners and hidden desktop icons stay as the theme set them: they are one setting for the whole Mac, and switching them costs seconds. The main display's Space decides for every display.
  • A Space you never go back to keeps the theme's wallpaper. macOS changes the desktop picture only on the Space on screen, so after a theme goes off each other Space gets yours back the next time you switch to it.

Fixes

  • VoiceOver, from the blind tester's fourth round. Under VoiceOver the More entries stand in the menu-bar menu itself (in the submenu an arrow key read one entry and closed the menu). The "menu-bar icon not shown" warning no longer comes up under VoiceOver, whose Screen Curtain made the icon look hidden. In Settings the sidebar comes first, then the page; each page's parts are a pop-up with its own name (Themes section, Shader section, Camera section) instead of radio buttons called "Section"; the status line is one "Overlay on/off" without an unlabelled image; and "Show dock now" says what it did.
  • No more "control Finder" prompt every half minute, from a beta tester. The trash icon asks Finder whether the Trash is full; macOS's question about that came back with every poll until it was answered. Now it is asked once per launch, and a "Don't Allow" leaves Finder alone.
  • Spaces, from a beta tester. The Setup Assistant asks whether the theme goes on every Space or only the one you are on. Each Space's own wallpaper is read from macOS's wallpaper store before the theme sets one, so a Space RetroMac finds already wearing a theme picture gets its own back instead of macOS's default. Quitting RetroMac while other Spaces still show the theme's wallpaper says so first (they get theirs back only when shown while RetroMac runs).
  • Windows minimise down into the dock again with a second display beside the main one. A MacBook next to a monitor, sitting a little lower, counted as a display below it; the hidden Mac Dock went to the left edge, and every minimised window flew off to the left.
  • A tidier flyout and menu. The flyout keeps the everyday switches; Only on this Space, Dock only and TV Tube left it (Spaces and TV Tube stay in the menu-bar menu). The menu-bar menu has a More submenu for Dock Only, the Game Library, the Setup Assistant and Rescue Desktop.
  • Started from the disk image or Downloads, RetroMac offers to move itself to Applications (an older copy goes to the Trash, and the new one takes over). Run from the mounted DMG it had no menu-bar icon its user could find, and vanished from Finder's search once the DMG was gone.
  • Settings ▸ Shader ▸ On & Off says which themes keep the shader off. Switching the shader off while a theme is on is remembered for that theme and outranks "Turn the shader on when RetroMac launches" — which then looked broken. Listed under the switch now, with Turn On Again.
  • Keep my wallpaper. Settings ▸ Desktop ▸ Wallpaper, per theme: the theme leaves your desktop picture alone, so a live-wallpaper app or macOS's own dynamic one stays. Without it, almost any setting, a display or a Space change put the theme's picture back over yours.
  • RetroMac can always be reached. When macOS does not show its menu-bar icon (a full menu bar, the notch, or switched off under System Settings ▸ Menu Bar), RetroMac says so a few seconds after launch and offers a Dock icon; and opening RetroMac again from Applications opens Settings, also while a theme's dock and desktop are on screen. It used to look as if it had not started at all.
  • Dashboard dims every display again with the theme on chosen Spaces. RetroMac moved its windows to the main display's Space, the second display's dimming too, which then sat as a dark patch in the main display's corner while the main display stayed bright.
  • The second display keeps its own picture with the theme on chosen Spaces. With separate Spaces per display, the theme's picture went onto the second display's Space as well (it followed the main display), and that Space then got macOS's default back, not its own.
  • Quitting and Rescue Desktop put your wallpaper back for sure. It was set while the Mac's Dock restarted (and, on quitting, just before RetroMac exited) and was lost; the screen kept the theme's picture. Now the Dock and the Finder come back first, and the picture after.
  • Quitting puts the Mac back as Rescue Desktop does. Windows the title bars moved down or rolled up go back where they were, and the menu bar, the desktop icons and the Mac's Dock come back from their backups, not only the wallpaper, the look and the Dock.
  • The Control Strip and the dock sit in place after a theme switch. Placed while the Mac's Dock was still on its way out, the System 7.1 and Mac OS 9 strip stayed a Dock's height up (and a dock off-centre) until the theme was chosen again.
  • Mountain Lion's dock is closer to the original. Silver-grey glass measured off the real shelf, rounded at the back corners too, mirroring the icons more; the running lights are blue-white glows on the lit front edge; Mountain Lion's own Trash, empty and full; and Launchpad straight after Finder, with its rocket the size of Safari's compass, opening the Launchpad's own screen — without hopping, as Launchpad never did.
  • Green Lite, and no blank screen without Screen Recording. A green phosphor terminal joins Amber Lite and B&W Lite, all three through macOS's colour filters, so no permission. And when a full shader is switched on without Screen Recording, its Lite version shows meanwhile instead of nothing, until the permission is granted (an idea from mac-crt).
  • Two new screensavers, and the Windows ones native. 3D Maze (the brick maze with its rats and the smiley) and 3D Text (your words or the time, in chrome, marble or wood) join the list, and 3D Pipes, 3D FlowerBox and Starfield Simulation now run natively instead of in a browser engine — lighter on the battery, at most 30 fps on battery. All five are retro-screensavers by Adrian Herskind (MIT), as RetroMac's own screensaver and as .saver modules for System Settings.
  • Mountain Lion's Apple menu and About This Mac. The black Apple opens 10.8's menu row for row (About This Mac, Software Update, App Store, System Preferences, Dock, Recent Items, Force Quit, Sleep, Restart, Shut Down, Log Out with your name), drawn white with the blue highlight. About This Mac is 10.8's window — its grey title bar, its buttons, the silver apple — with this Mac's own version, processor, memory and startup disk.
  • Mountain Lion magnifies like Snow Leopard, switched under Settings ▸ Dock ▸ Magnification on hover or the Apple menu's Dock submenu, and has the Downloads stack: the newest files piled up on the dock icon as large as the icons beside it, changing as downloads arrive, and the grid of them on a click with Open in Finder as its last tile. No Applications folder, as in 10.8.
  • Launchpad, Mountain Lion's. A click on its tile fades the desktop picture in blurred over the whole screen, with a search field at the top (Return opens the first match), your apps as large icons eight across and five down, page dots under them (click them, swipe, scroll or use the arrow keys), the dock still on top. Escape, a click beside the icons or the tile again closes it, and the app you were in comes back.
  • VoiceOver, from the blind tester's third round. Switching themes no longer leaves the arrows, Return and Esc held for the whole Mac — with a drawn menu or the Start menu open at the switch they stayed RetroMac's, and VoiceOver's own menu bar and menus stopped answering until RetroMac was force-quit. The shader shortcut says "Shader on" or "Shader off". The Control Strip's scroll arrows say which modules came into view. Shader, Live Wallpaper, Virtual Camera, Retro Viewport and TV Tube in the menu read as switches with their state, and the Shader / Live Wallpaper choice as radio buttons (an unnamed image before). ⌘W and Esc reach Settings and the readme while another of RetroMac's windows holds the keyboard, and the Settings footer reads "Overlay on, auto fps" instead of an unnamed image. ⌘W and Esc now really close Settings: its SwiftUI view used both keys up before the menu saw them (Close Window worked from the menu, never from the keys). The menu-bar icon opens its menu again after VoiceOver closed it (a press through accessibility brings no event, and was taken for the click that had just closed it). In More, Dock Only and Rescue Desktop come last: VoiceOver with Quick Nav opened More on Dock Only and set it off, which restarted the Finder. TV Tube says which channel is on when it opens and at every Up or Down, and how to work it the first time. Found with RetroMac's accessibility tree on System 7.1: the "empty system dialogue" VoiceOver kept landing in was the window of the menu bar's Apple — now the Apple menu button where the theme has one, and no window at all where it does not; the Application menu and Balloon Help in the menu bar have names. After a boot screen the app that was in front gets the keyboard back — RetroMac stayed in front with no window to type into, and the keys went nowhere. While VoiceOver runs, a theme leaves the menu bar shown, so RetroMac's own item stays in reach. The menu says which theme is on after a launch that turned it on (it said "Off"). Settings' sections are one "Section" pop-up to VoiceOver, saying which one is open; as radio buttons VoiceOver always entered on the first.
  • "Turn the shader on when RetroMac launches" works with "Activate theme on launch". The theme coming on at launch marked the shader as running without starting it, so the launch switch skipped it and every shader switch read on while the screen was plain; under VoiceOver the theme's own preset was skipped too.
  • VoiceOver, from a blind tester's second round. The Control Strip, the docks, the Start menus and the panels keep each control as the same element between VoiceOver's questions; built anew each time, VoiceOver stopped after the second one (the Control Strip's Scroll left) and read the tree again and again. At first launch the onboarding hints are readable with Next, Skip and GitHub buttons instead of an empty dialog, and RetroMac no longer asks for Automation by itself (it asks on Grant, or when a theme hides the menu bar), so macOS's prompt is not buried. Boot screens are skipped while VoiceOver runs: a full-screen picture that took the focus for five seconds. Removing an app from a list puts VoiceOver on the next one, and the Settings tabs are no longer read with "Settings" in front.
  • The menu-bar icon opens and closes its menu reliably. The menu is popped up by the icon instead of hanging on it, and the click that closes it is recognised as that same click — not by a quarter-second window, which also swallowed a quick deliberate reopen. Mountain Lion's dock sits on the bottom edge of the screen, as 10.8's did.
  • Mountain Lion's dock is Mountain Lion's. It was a flat rounded bar with dark dots. Now it is the 10.8 shelf: frosted glass running back in perspective, a darker front face under a lit edge, reflections that end on the glass, and running apps shown as small glowing lights set into the front edge. On the side of the screen it is smoked glass.
  • Windows themes: minimising is quick and looks like Windows. Only the title bar flies into the taskbar button, in a fifth of a second, as Windows animated it; the whole window used to squash into the button over twice as long. Windows XP has Claude and ChatGPT icons (the Windows 7 art).
  • Windows themes: a minimised window flies into its taskbar button. It used to shrink towards wherever the hidden Mac Dock kept that app, a different place for every app. Now the title bar's minimise box, ⌘M and a click on the active window's taskbar button all send the window into its own button. A window that has no button yet minimises the Mac's way.
  • Rescue Desktop reaches every Space. With the theme on chosen Spaces, the other Spaces kept RetroMac's wallpaper after a rescue or after turning the theme off, because nothing handed them back when you switched to them. They get your own picture back on the first visit again.
  • Claude, Chrome and ChatGPT wear the theme's icon in Mac OS 9.2 Classic and Mountain Lion (the Mac OS 9 and Snow Leopard art), and Chrome in Windows XP. ChatGPT now reports itself as com.openai.codex; every theme that dresses com.openai.chat dresses it too.
  • Boot screens fill the screen. A 16:9 boot screen on a 16:10 display (a MacBook) had black bars above and below; it now fills the display and loses a few percent of plain background at its sides. Mac OS 9.2 Classic's clip had black bars inside the video itself, now cut away. Windows 95 and Windows Me boot in 16:9: their 4:3 pictures are widened, not enlarged — the sky and the white continue at the sides and the progress bar runs the full width.
  • Folders in the Snow Leopard dock reflect too. A reflection used to start at the edge of the picture file; a folder stands on transparent rows (about an eighth of its height), so the fade had nearly run out before the folder showed. It now starts at the picture's visible bottom.
  • Futurama's web-app windows close again. Their close button was drawn but no click reached it; every window style now hands its buttons to the same tracker.
  • Scanline and glass-reflection overlays draw again. Settings ▸ Shader offered Light, Medium, Heavy and Subtle, Strong under names the overlay code did not know, so every choice drew nothing. The two shortcut rows "Cycle effect preset" and "Bump intensity" are gone: they recorded a key but nothing ever listened for it.
  • The wallpaper follows every Space. A theme's picture used to land only on the Space you were on, and turning the theme off gave only that Space its picture back; the others kept the theme's for good. Now each Space shows the theme's picture once you switch to it, and gets its own picture back the same way, the one it had, not one picture for the whole screen.
  • The Rescue Desktop report shows RetroMac's icon, so it is not taken for a message from macOS, and has Don't show this again for a rescue that simply worked; one that fails or needs a permission is still shown. Settings ▸ Shortcuts ▸ Rescue Desktop turns it back on.
  • Dock reflections follow the icon. In Snow Leopard a magnified icon kept the small reflection of its resting size, off to one side, and every reflection faded the wrong way: faint under the icon, strongest at the screen edge, where it was cut off. Now the reflection grows with the icon, is brightest right under it and fades out on the shelf. A full Trash reflects as full.
  • Amiga Workbench and SGI IRIX hide the Mac's menu bar, as the Windows themes do. Their own bars sit at the top of the screen (Workbench's title bar with its clock, IRIX's Toolchest and Shelf), and the menu bar covered them.
  • Settings are easier to find. Themes comes first in the sidebar, General before Shortcuts. The Shader settings are four tabs instead of a Section menu: Presets & Effects, Screen & Apps, Performance, On & Off. Retro Mode is called Favourite now, which is what it is: your favourite look in one click.
  • The Setup Assistant is shorter (580 instead of 700 points), and its theme list is grouped by Apple, Windows, Unix & Amiga and Other, folded until opened. The menu's Themes submenu now files Solaris, QNX and NeXTSTEP under Unix & Amiga instead of Other.
  • Theme switches no longer restart the Dock and Finder for nothing. The theme's Finder and window tweaks were written again, and both restarted, on every wallpaper pass (several per theme switch, and on every display change), even when nothing had changed. Now only a real change restarts them.
  • VoiceOver no longer lists RetroMac's drawing as windows. The shader, the title bars and their lights over every app window and the window animations showed up as untitled, empty windows in VoiceOver's Window Chooser. They are left out now; the dock, desktop, panels, widgets and settings stay in.
  • VoiceOver can use the themes. The theme windows have names (Dock, Desktop, Front Panel, Shelf, Taskbar, Deskbar, Control Strip …), and what they hold are buttons and menu items with their names that VoiceOver can press: dock items (running apps by their name, no longer their bundle id, in the tooltip too), desktop icons, the Start button, Start menus, clock and tray, taskbar window buttons, the CDE Front Panel and its subpanels, the Photon shelf and taskbar, the BeOS Deskbar, the NeXT dock, the Control Strip, the IRIX Toolchest and the theme menus. Dragging (moving icons and windows, resizing the Control Strip) and the Mac OS 9 volume slider have no VoiceOver form yet.
  • The themes by keyboard. ⌃Esc opens the theme's main menu (Start, the Apple menu, the Be menu, the Workspace Menu, Launch, the NeXT menu, the Toolchest; Program Manager on Windows 3.1). In every menu RetroMac draws, the arrow keys move the highlight, → and Return open a submenu, ← closes it, Return chooses and Esc closes, however the menu was opened. ⌃⇧Esc moves into the dock or taskbar: ← → go from item to item under a focus ring, Return opens, Esc leaves, and ⌃⇧Esc again goes on to the next bar. VoiceOver says the highlighted entry. Both shortcuts are in Settings ▸ Shortcuts ▸ Keyboard access; one that is already yours is not taken.
  • Automation can be granted. The released app could never send Apple Events (an entitlement was missing under the hardened runtime), so macOS never asked, RetroMac never appeared under Automation, and Grant only opened an empty pane. Grant now brings up macOS's own prompt; System Settings opens only after an earlier refusal.
  • ⌘W and Esc close RetroMac's windows (Settings, readmes, Setup, What's New, the Game Library), and ⌘C/⌘V work in all of them.
  • More for VoiceOver: the Settings sidebar and the Shader tabs are a group of tabs, the effect scope is three radio buttons, the drawn panels (Control Strip, Front Panel, Deskbar …) no longer read "content is empty", RetroMac's own decoration no longer announces "new window", the Applications window and the dock's stacks are named with their items as buttons, decorative pictures are left out and icon-only buttons have names. Every switch reads as a switch ("switch, on"), no longer as a "toggle button". The title-bar list shows Pac-Man by name.
  • The dock magnifies when the pointer comes down from the menu bar, not only after another app's window was clicked: while RetroMac was the active app the dock heard the pointer enter and leave but none of the moves in between.
  • A second click on RetroMac's menu-bar icon closes its menu instead of opening it again at once.
  • On a Space without the theme the Mac's Dock is there after launch too; the theme hid it again right after the Space had shown it.
  • No more log file on the Desktop. The retro dock wrote every show and hide to retromac_dock.log on your Desktop. Those lines now go to About ▸ Diagnostics, and only with the new Debug logging switch there, which is off unless you turn it on.
  • BeOS gets title bars: the yellow tab, only as wide as the window's title, with the close box on the left and the zoom box on the right; grey on windows behind; a double-click hides the window. Part of the experimental title bars.
  • The BeOS readme has a real BeOS window: the yellow tab sits on the frame with the close box and the zoom box, and beside it the desktop shows through.
  • Pac-Man could not start. A build machine without SDL2_ttf and SDL2_mixer (Homebrew dropped them when it moved SDL2 onto SDL3) left an empty game in the app, 2.8.8 included, and a click on Pac-Man did nothing. A release build now stops instead, and an app without the game hides it rather than offering it.
  • No theme title bar over Reframe or Pac-Man, which draw their own retro window: each goes on the title-bar exclusion list once (Reframe when it is installed). Take it off there to change that.
  • The Start button stays pressed while its menu is open, as on every Windows from 95 to 7.
  • WindowShade never loses a window. A rolled-up window keeps its way back until it is really back: an app that does not answer leaves it rolled up, to be unrolled again, and on a theme switch or at quit it stays on record for the next start if it would not move. A theme switch right after rolling up can no longer send the window away again, and the recovery after a crash no longer waits seconds on a hung app.
  • Fix: a wallpaper that could not be set was taken as set, so the next pass skipped it.
  • Fix: the Mac OS X pill rolls windows up on a laptop screen again. macOS keeps a window's last 52 points on a single display; the strip left at the edge is one point wide, and that no longer counts as "still in view" and sends the window straight back.
  • Fix: desktop icons no longer sit under the dock. Its window reaches higher than the bar (room for magnified icons and names) and swallowed the clicks on any icon down there, the Screen Saver under Mac OS X among them. Icons now keep above it and move on to the next column when a screen is too short, as the Finder did.
  • Mission Control and Exposé no longer show the title bars as little windows of their own.
  • Choosing a printer in the Control Strip no longer pauses the strip.
  • Rescue Desktop brings the menu bar back when a theme or the menu-bar shortcut hid it, and says so if macOS would not let it.
  • The shader is off behind the lock screen and while the displays sleep. "Stop overlay on sleep or lock" now covers both; after unlocking or waking it comes back as the effect it was (Live Wallpaper stays Live Wallpaper), if set to resume.

item.title: Version 2.2
item.description:
RetroMac 2.2: please update manually, one time

This release includes a technical change to how updates are delivered, so your copy can’t install it automatically. Please download 2.2 from the button below and drag it into your Applications folder, just this once. After that, automatic updates work as normal again.

  • Authentic Mac System 6: true 1-bit black & white theme.
  • Warcraft I + II: play them natively with your own game data.
  • Mac OS X boot animation for the Mac OS X and Snow Leopard themes.
  • Clearer Pro unlocks and assorted polish.
